utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning. Yes, Mr. Black, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think you customarily also remind the witness of his oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Witness, let me take this opportunity to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of the -- your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the end of the day yesterday we were talking a little bit about the end of August 1990 and the barricades, so I am going to continue with that topic, okay?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for something from the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, of course, don't know what questions the Prosecutor is going to ask, but if he asks questions about territory of the former Yugoslavia, I would like to be given a map of the former Yugoslavia so that we don't speak about an imaginary country, but that we are all able to see what it looked like on the ground, if it's possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just wait for the questions, and I'm sure the Prosecutor will attend to that problem if and when the need arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hadn't intended to ask any questions that would require a map, but if I do, I'm sure one can be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, if you think you need a map, you can ask for one, although as I said, I don't think it is going to be necessary. So let me go back to August 1990 and the barricades which we were talking about at the end of the day yesterday. You suggested in the first part of your testimony, in your direct examination, that the barricades were initially erected spontaneously, but then later they were organised and you said because so many barricades were causing communication problems. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also testified that on the 17th of August, 1990, and the two or three days after that, you personally participated in organising and coordinating the barricades until Milan Babic relieved you of that duty a couple of days after the 17th; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was at the warning centre, and there I was in communication with the barricades or the roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think the words that you used on Monday were that you were the unofficial -- an unofficial commander of the barricades during that; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the term only conditionally. I was the deputy commander of the Crisis Staff, because in the state of an emergency you set up a Crisis Staff, that's according to the statute of the municipality, and because President Babic was not present in Knin at the time, I had to take his place and perform these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in fact, from the 17th of August, 1990, Milan Babic was -- excuse me, Milan Martic, I apologise, was in command of the barricades, right, from -- already from the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to -- I'm going to read to you --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know that Mr. Babic replaced me on the third day. But as I told you, Mr. Prosecutor, I did not take note of the dates or anything, but I think that is how it was. On the third day, I was relieved of my duty, and Milan Babic phoned me and told me that I replaced, I said fine, and I no longer had anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you a couple of more questions about what you've just said. And first, I would like to show you -- I would actually like to show you part of Exhibit 496 in evidence. Mr. Macura, this is an interview Milan Martic gave to the BBC in October of 1994. Hopefully in a moment we can see it on our screens and I will show you the part that I'm interested in. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I think another button needs to be pushed like a broadcast button so that it's actually e-court that we're seeing on the screen. Right now we're seeing the e-court version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking above me, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I was trying to assist the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't need to do anything on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We shouldn't need to do anything, Your Honour. It is just the regular e-court button, that's what we need to press. I apologise for the confusion. Actually, the particular page I would like to look at is -- has at the top 02195509. I think it is about the sixth page. Just a moment, Mr. Macura. We're having some technical issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all right. No problem. No problem. Just do your job. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have a technical problem with e-court and the technician will be coming to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Should we just wait for a moment. Is it going to be right away or should I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's just wait for a moment and hopefully he will be coming almost right away. Or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: He will be coming any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may help? If you have an original in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem. We don't have a need for your help, Mr. Macura. It is not a question of language. It is a question of technology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, do you have something on your screen now? Can you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] United Nations. Now United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's not it. Let's see if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't know if this is of assistance, but if we can make sure that the Defence and the accused and the witness have it, then we can certainly get by on the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like it is going to take a little longer to repair the problem. Maybe we should take a break and come back at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 9.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just when we thought everything was fine, our reporter reports that LiveNote has gone down. Can somebody help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Sorry about all of that inconvenience. Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Technology is a blessing and a curse sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem with it is when it collapses, then you are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's exactly right. I think we have it sorted out now. So on the e-court we have the B/C/S version now visible to the witness, and if we could turn to page 6, please, of the B/C/S version. In the English I think we're seeing the right page. It's the one that ends in ERN 5509. To page 6 of the B/C/S is what we need to see. This is -- page 1 is what I see right now and we need to go to page 6. Yes. Perfect. If we could scroll down to the -- a little further please, yes. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, now you see on the screen in front of you the transcript of this interview which, again, I remind you it was an interview give by Milan Martic to the BBC in October of 1994. And in this paragraph you can see he talks about the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think maybe it will be easiest if I just read out this paragraph, and you follow along with me. It says: "On the 17th of August, two days before our referendum, we got an info that Croatia with its police had started to disarm the police stations in Serbian opstinas. In Knin we allowed them to disarm us. In agreement with Raskovic and Babic, we decided to take all the weapons from the storages of the reserve militia and we made a false attempt as if the citizens broke into the storage. We took the arms and from that moment I personally assumed command over the roadblocks." Do you accept that, Mr. Macura, that on the 17th of August, Mr. Martic assumed command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Mr. Macura your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, this is not correct. This is simply not correct. I was replaced on the third day. I did not sleep for two days, and then I was replaced on the third day. And then I took my children halfway from Knin to Bosnia for them to remain there and then I went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you were replaced on the third day, from which day? When was the first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was replaced on the 19th. I spent two nights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, is it possible that in those days, when you tell us that you were in charge, that you were in charge in the political sense, while Mr. Martic was in charge of the barricades in an operational sense. Is that a possible distinction?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not possible. That is not possible. I was in charge of the roadblocks in any sense, because I was the deputy commander of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Babic, so I was absolutely in charge of the barricades. And on the third day, Babic replaced me, and from then on I had nothing to do with the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So in your view, at least would you accept that Martic was in charge of the barricades after that day when you were relieved of your duties. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic told me that I was replaced. And apparently he then appointed Milan Martic, but he didn't tell me that. And he told me I was relieved of my duties, and I asked him whether I could then go home and he says, yes, fine, you can go home now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You say that he didn't tell you that. But did you know or did you learn that Babic had put Martic in charge of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did learn that at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, when you mentioned the Crisis Staff, is that the same thing as what could be called the Staff for the Defence of Knin? Or is that a different body?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is the civilian body. It's a civilian authority that is set up in any state of emergency or any emergency situation, floods, any kind of natural disaster. It has nothing to do with the police. And somebody from those structures can, of course, be involved in the work of the Crisis Staff, but that is up to the people in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe my question wasn't perfectly clear. Did you hear about something called the Staff for Defence of Knin which was then later renamed the Council for National Resistance. Are you familiar with that body?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that at the beginning. Later on, there were some communiques over the radio, signed by that body, but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you never heard or learned that that body operated from Golubic and had a role in the organisation and the coordination of the barricades at some point?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a police school in Golubic later on, but I don't know anything about this Council for National Resistance that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Since you mentioned police, you testified that sometime after the 17th, 18th and 19th of August, 1990, that the police took over the operation of the barricades. I think what you said was that the barricades were removed and check-points were set up. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. That is how it was, because there were too many roadblocks and only -- the police check-points were set up at only a few places, and I had nothing to do with them at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. The police at those check-points, as you call them, they wore uniforms and wore their regular weapons, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not right at the beginning, but only later on. And I can't really recall the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the subject of weapons. You testified a little bit about Croatia obtaining weapons from Hungary. It's true, isn't it, that on the 17th of August, 1990, as we saw in this interview, Martic and others organised the removal of the reserve police weapons from the Knin police station and they distributed those weapons to Serbs at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what Mr. Martic says, I believe that it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, and you -- you had at least heard that yourself at the time, didn't you? Did you know anything about this at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had my regular job, my regular tasks. And I had heard thousands of stories during the war and I cannot really talk about that now in court. I cannot say anything about it. There were rumours that there had been people killed here and there, and I tried to calm people down over the radio, not to panic. There weren't any people killed. And I even sent people to check whether any Serbs had really been killed at Osijek and they are verified that no one had been killed there, and you know how things just spiral out of control in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. This was actually something that Milan Babic knew about, because Babic went to Golubic and saw Martic distributing these weapons. Milan Babic never mentioned this to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic never told me anything about any distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to events of 1991, so I'm moving ahead a little bit in time. You mentioned a conflict in Plitvice on Easter of 1991. Do you remember testifying briefly about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I passed through that road a couple of hours before the clash, through Plitvice. I was driving from Vojnic in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes you explained that yesterday and I don't need you to repeat it now. But the conflict, the clash in Plitvice, that was actually started when Serb policemen entered the area, which then provoked a response from the Croatian police, and that's how fighting started. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. I don't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, it's not really a question, I don't think, of how it is seen. It's true that the Serb police moved into Plitvice before this fighting started, and then the Croatian police responded to that, and that's how the fighting broke out. Is that a correct chronology?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Plitvice is the Serb territory with a Serb majority, and the police station was set up in Sabarsko, and troops were masked there, police forces from Croatia, and I don't know who went in where. I really can't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So don't really know who went in where first?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I will move on to something else, then. And it's something that you just mentioned. I think you were referring, when you mentioned Saborsko. You said during your testimony that Croatia set up new police stations in places like Kijevo and Saborsko in 1991.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They brought in a large force, with the intent of attacking Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you don't really know what their intent was, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why else would they bring in such large forces into a police station for any other reason? I really can't see any other reason, except an attack that they wanted to launch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But just so that I am clear. That's just your sort of speculation about their motives, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can say that this is my speculation, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There was nothing unlawful about Croatia establishing new police stations within its territory, right, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was unlawful or lawful, but I think that their intentions were bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But wasn't it understandable that they would create police stations in places like Kijevo and Saborsko, which were Croat villages surrounded by Serb-controlled territory, given the tensions in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one attacked Saborsko or Kijevo. Neither Saborsko nor Kijevo had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Kijevo was attacked by Serb police and by the JNA in August of 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that happened in Kijevo. There was an attack later on, but I don't remember whether it was indeed in August. But at that time the Croatian forces were already deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. And Saborsko was attacked by the JNA TO and police in November of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. That's possible, but the Croatian forces were already there. The village of Saborsko, the civilians were not attacked. The attack was launched on the Croatian forces that were masked there. It was a military operation, at least that's what the Serb officers say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But you didn't participate in that, you don't really know what happened in Saborsko, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, of course not. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing that you testified about in 1991 -- well, actually, the date is something I want to ask you about. You testified about a ZNG parade in a stadium in Zagreb, and you said you thought this occurred in 1990. Do you remember the parade that I'm talking about in that stadium?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I remember seeing it on TV because the Croatian TV did broadcast this event, but I don't remember the date. And I have to apologise to the Court, I never thought that I would have to write down the dates. But at any rate, this was not a secret. This was shown on TV, in order for even greater effect to be achieved, both on the Croat people and on the Serb people. In fact, this was the -- an act of the establishment of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Would you accept that that parade actually took place at the end of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't say that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because the ZNG wasn't even formed until May 1991, was it? So it couldn't have been -- there couldn't have been a ZNG parade before May, because May 1991 is when it was created.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I trust that you are right. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing about the ZNG, you said that it was set up by the HDZ, but in fact it was the Croatian government that established the ZNG, not the party itself, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political party formed the government, the political party dictated all the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you agree with me that as it actually the government, the Croatian government that set up the ZNG. It wasn't -- they weren't armed forces of the party. They were a force of the government, Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may be right, but the HDZ initiated all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move now to the delegation which you participated in, that went to Belgrade to announce the results of the referendum from April or May 1991. Do you know the topic that I'm focused on now? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only ask you whether you're referring to the second referendum?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. The 1991 referendum.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the delegation, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. A little bit kind of background of this referendum. On the 1st of April, 1991, the SAO Krajina Executive Council had actually taken a decision to annex Krajina to Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the question at the referendum was: Are you in favour of Krajina remaining in Yugoslavia and for the unification of SAO Krajina with Serbia? I think that this is exactly how the question was worded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What I was asking you was about something slightly different. Before the referendum on the 1st of April, 1991, do you remember that there was a decision of the SAO Krajina Executive Council taking the decision to annex Krajina to Serbia? This is an agreed fact among the parties in this case. Do you remember that that happened, or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was. Mr. Milan Babic was the chairman of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And on the basis of that decision on the 1st of April, it was on the 30th of April, 1991, that there was the decision to hold the referendum with the question essentially as you stated it, right, that was the chronology?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would just note that that decision of the 30th of April is Exhibit 148. Actually, if we could show Exhibit 148 on the screen, just so the witness has a chance to see it, please. Thank you. That's perfect. If we could just look at -- scroll down a little bit to article 3. Yeah, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, you will see there that it says the question to be answered at the referendum is: "Are you in favour of the accession of Krajina to the Republic of Serbia and of Krajina's staying in Yugoslavia with Serbia Montenegro and others who wish to preserve Yugoslavia?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Something has now popped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise. I went too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, this is - this is essentially the question as you remember it; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I remember that in a slightly different form but now I can see the exact wording, but the essence is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's all for that exhibit. Mr. Macura, in fact Slobodan Milosevic reacted quite strongly to the decision on the 1st of April about annexing Krajina to Serbia and he even asked Milan Babic to withdraw that decision, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Slobodan Milosevic was absolutely against such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Milosevic asked that the referendum question be framed in terms of supporting Yugoslavia rather than mentioning annexation to Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic wouldn't hear of a decision about its annexation to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that was because Mr. Milosevic's strategy was to arrive at his political goals of uniting Serbs in Yugoslavia but not in such an openly public way. Publicly he insisted that the rhetoric be about preserving Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your conclusion, and that is not my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your impression, Mr. Macura?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My impression is that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic did not, at all, want any annexation of Krajina to Serbia, as is written here. And my impression is that he did not associate the Krajina with Serbia in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not a question. The question put to you is that it was Mr. Milosevic's strategy that the rhetoric should not mention annexation to Serbia, but it must be seen to be annexation to -- to maintain Yugoslavia as a unit. That's the question. What's your impression on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. Macura, that we're getting hung up on the word "annexation," but you agree with me, don't you, that Mr. Milosevic was in favour of the idea of all Serbs living in one common state, be it called Yugoslavia or by some other name. He was in favour of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He advocated that, counting on Yugoslavia's survival. But later, he abandoned the idea. He did not want Yugoslavia to be brought down as a state first and foremost, that was his basic strategy. But it was aborted. He failed in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In 1991, in May of 1991, the time we're talking about, he still -- still subscribed to this goal of all Serbs living in one common state, be it Yugoslavia or another one, right, that was still his position then?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal position seeing that we all were living in one state and we wanted to remain in it. I, too, wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, but not to live in Belgrade. I wanted to remain in it, living in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when is it that you say that Milosevic abandoned this idea?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon, I believe. From what I heard from the lady journalist, Mila Stula, who was close to the leadership, the Hotel Moskava in Belgrade, and I had a lengthy talk with Mila Stula, this lady journalist who was close to political and leadership circles, and she asserted that Mr. Milosevic had practically renounced the Krajina in agreement with Tudjman and that he had done this, that they had done this in Karadjordjevo. But I cannot really tell you the date. This was quite early on. She referred to that. Also, to the fact, and I don't know whether it is true, that Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman were talking about a division of Bosnia, and in that option, the Krajina had to remain in Croatia definitely. There could be no word of the Krajina's remaining in Serbia, or of any such agreement being struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But this was all later. This was after 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that it was that much later, because already in 1992 we have the United Nations deployed in the Krajina, so that it couldn't have been that much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that in April and May -- in April and May 1991 Serbia was providing support to the Krajina in several ways, including the training centre at Golubic which you've mentioned, weapons, and other kinds of support to the Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the refusal to -- to receive your delegation, about the referendum, that didn't interfere with those other kinds of support, did it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information whatsoever about that, because I was not a part of those circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You were asked a couple of questions yesterday or the day before about peace talks in The Hague in September 1991. Do you remember that topic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in September 1991, and I myself was in The Hague as a member of a delegation attending those talks. I believe the Presidency of Yugoslavia, its members had arrived to The Hague before that, and then the later they invited us also. Mr. Babic, Milan Babic was there. Dr. Smilja Avramov was there, I myself was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to interrupt you. We don't need to go into that, indeed, specifically. But the purpose of that peace conference was to consider the so-called Carrington Plan, correct, which was a plan to globally consider the issues happening in Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so there is no confusion, the Vance Plan came later and it was specific to Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you a couple of questions about the Vance Plan. You told us that Cyrus Vance went to Slobodan Milosevic to negotiate the plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is correct, because after that Slobodan Milosevic brought pressure to bear on Mr. Babic to accept the plan. But I did not see Mr. Vance go and visit Mr. Milosevic, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But it would make sense that Vance would go -- speak with Milosevic because Milosevic was recognised as the leader of the Serbs in Yugoslavia at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And it's also correct that the negotiations for the Vance Plan were between Mr. Vance, Milosevic, Veljko Kadijevic, and Franjo Tudjman. Those were the people who really negotiated the plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know the exact composition of the delegation representing the Yugoslav side. But given the offices which they held, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember that the first real step towards agreement of the Vance Plan was a cease-fire that was signed by those four people on the 23rd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of cease-fires and a number of cease-fire agreements, but they were frequently violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If I could show a document on the e-court, please. And the document ID number is 01198871. That's the first page of the ERN range. This is a document I believe we only have in English. I'm not sure if any --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. We have nothing on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I don't either. We need to see -- I don't know if they're having trouble finding it. The ERN number again is 01198871 to 8873. And it's a document that's only in English, so we will all need to see the English on the -- on our monitors. You know, it's possible that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have the document in our inbox. I'm sorry. We haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's my apologies. I thought this was being uploaded this morning. I brought hard copies just in case, so we will do it the old-fashioned way. My apologies, Your Honour. With the assistance of the usher, we have copies for everyone, the witness, Defence counsel, and the Bench, thank you. My apologies to the registrar for leading her on a wild goose chase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you can see that this is a United Nations Security Council document. And if you look at -- if you look at the fourth paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, can it be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. If we can put one on the ELMO, please. Yes, thank you. Actually we'll be flipping pages so if the usher wouldn't mind standing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you can see towards the bottom of the page, there is a paragraph that starts: "On Saturday, 23rd November ..."

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, I can see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And it says -- it talks about Mr. Vance convening a meeting with Mr. Vance, President Milosevic, President Tudjman and General Kadijevic. And then the last line of that says: "The parties reached an agreement, the signed text of which is attached to the present letter." You see that, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can just then look at the last page in the document, page 3. There we see the signatures of Milosevic, Tudjman, Kadijevic and Cyrus Vance; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So this, this is essentially the November 1991 cease-fire agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be Exhibit 948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm assuming we want to stick to the usual schedule, despite the slight delay this morning. It would be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's do that, because then we don't get out of kilter with our schedule. We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, just before the break, we had taken a look at that November 1991 cease-fire agreement. And it was on the basis of that agreement that then the details were sort of worked out. And in February of 1992, the United Nations Security Council adopted a resolution which provided for the deployment of UN peacekeepers, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time of these negotiations at the end of 1991, Slobodan Milosevic, he was not a member of the SFRY federal government, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Milosevic didn't consult with Krajina leaders in his negotiations with Mr. Vance and the others, did he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he had no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What do you mean by "he had no need to"?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic could only issue orders to the Krajina, rather than consult with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And the Krajina leadership later complained about that lack of consultation, including at the SFRY Presidency sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krajina leadership was in a subordinated position, but had no one to complain to. I don't know how do you mean that. How you mean that, to complain to whom? Because Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bora Jovic were two of a kind. They shared -- they had a shared opinion. Bora -- sorry, Bora Jovic was at the federal level and Slobodan Milosevic at the republican level, that of Serbia. We had no one to complain to, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, what I mean -- you yourself talked about Krajina leaders going to Belgrade to a meeting with members of the SFRY Presidency, and you talked about the discussions there, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. And actually, we were being imposed a solution that we were against, but it was imposed on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But what I meant to say was that the Krajina leadership, at those Presidency sessions, they voiced their discontent. They complained about the fact that they hadn't been consulted, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, because we were talking about our own mix.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified a little bit yesterday and maybe the day before about the attitude of Serbia and the remainder of Yugoslavia towards the Krajina Serbs, so I want to ask you a couple of questions about that. First, you referred to a meeting of the SFRY Presidency. Did you personally attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I personally attended that meeting, and there were many of us at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you remember the date or even the month of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that, but it was certainly after this cease-fire agreement, when already actions aimed at toppling the government of Milan Babic were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, it was certainly after November 1991 --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it couldn't have been any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was associated with the Vance Plan. It was directly connected with the Vance Plan, with its acceptance, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So it probably would have been in December or January, December 1991 or January 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if you were recorded in the minutes as being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't check it. I was probably recorded in the minutes as attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any reason why your name wouldn't appear on the minutes? So that if I, or someone else, were to go look through those minutes of the sessions from December and January, is there any reason why you might not appear there, that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of any reason why I shouldn't feature on the minutes, in the minutes, but if someone had that kind of a reason, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Serb leaders, both in Serbia and in the federal government of Yugoslavia, they had several reasons for supporting the Vance Plan, and they explained some of those reasons at the Presidency session, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they gave us guarantees that they would be the ones to protect the Serbs in the Krajina. In military terms, that would have been the Yugoslav People's Army. So that they reassured us that we would be completely protected by the UNPROFOR and by the JNA, which was a right of Knin, 15 or 20 kilometres from Knin in Grahovo. And that is quite near the border with Bosnia, as is Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just focus for a second on the reasons why Serbia and the Yugoslav authorities supported the Vance Plan. They thought, really, that there were only two alternatives at that point: Accept the Vance Plan, or continue with the war. That was the way they saw the two alternatives, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Serbia, in particular, was not enthusiastic about continuing with the war, right, in part because there was an anti-war movement in Serbia at that time, which opposed the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was rather on account of external factors, because at the talks which we had with Mr. Jovanovic, who was the foreign minister at the time, he told us that they were being threatened, that Belgrade was being threatened with bombing, if the conflicts in Croatia continued. So that I believe that it was rather on account of these external pressures than on account of the internal situation that that was so, although it is quite possible that some internal movement could have been of bearing on that position, even though Mr. Milosevic had things on internal scene under very good control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Then you mentioned external pressures. Milosevic and some others in Serbia in the leadership of Serbia and of Yugoslavia, they thought that rejecting the Vance Plan would make -- make it look like the Serbs were not really interested in peace, that they were rejecting a peaceful solution. That was the way they perceived this, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. That is also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that expressed to you and other Krajina leaders?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have mentioned General Adzic, who actually grabbed Mr. Stikovac by the neck to strangulate him, and he said to him, as I told you: You Knin riff-raff, you see what the entire state has to go through on your account.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that before. But I'm really focused on isn't it true that this was one of the reasons that was put forth to you as an explanation by the federal and the Serbian leaders, that they didn't want to reject the Vance Plan and thereby allow the accusation against them, that Serbs were rejecting peaceful solutions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, is that something that you remember from the Presidency session which you attended?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the essence of it was that Yugoslavia did not want to be Krajina's victim, to be hostage to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that means that, really, Yugoslavia was facing a lot of pressures from the international community and they didn't want to be forced into rejecting the Vance Plan, because that would have undermined their position vis-a-vis the international community, right, that was their reasoning?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another factor in the thinking of the Serbian and the Yugoslav authorities was, they thought that by accepting the Vance Plan, the Serbs in Krajina would also have a chance to consolidate the political and territorial gains which they had made in 1990 and 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, because they guaranteed to us that the Yugoslavia's laws would be applied on Krajina's territory. That was guaranteed under the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so in light of sort of the reasons we talked about, it wouldn't be fair, would it, to say that Milosevic or Serbia or the Yugoslav authorities were abandoning Krajina by accepting the Vance Plan. They were simply taking a pragmatic decision based on what they thought was best under the circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan definitively amounted to an occupation of the Krajina. That was our opinion. I believe that the people in Belgrade were aware of that, too, but they were saying something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. I think you explained that before, about your view of the Vance Plan. And I was just interested in the characterisation of what Milosevic and the Serbian and Yugoslav authorities thought. It wouldn't be fair, would it, to say that they were abandoning Krajina by this decision, but that was their pragmatic decision under the circumstances, that the Vance Plan needed to be accepted and that you would work from there, sort of within that framework of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How is it that you disagree? What about what I said was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in is not about pragmatics. They knew that Krajina practically would not exist anymore, that it would have to be reinstituted within Croatia's borders, but they were actually deceiving the people and they were giving statements to that effect precisely with that purpose in mind, to deceive the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly not what they told you and the other Krajina leadership, right? Or are you saying they were trying to deceive you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what they told us, but they tried to deceive us, and we refused to accept this deception and that is why we had to be removed from the political arena.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This decision, which you say was imposed on you by Belgrade to accept the Vance Plan, that didn't signal the end of support, Serbian and Yugoslav support for the Krajina, did it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to pretend that they gave us support for a time. That's how I see it. Just in order to keep the people deceived for a little while longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't just a little while longer. For instance, even up until 1995 people in the SVK received their pay from the VJ, right, so that kind of support continued after the Vance Plan was accepted.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this pay was really very low, it was miserable. It wasn't something that you could live on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'm correct, aren't I, that the -- there was also other kinds of economic support that were provided besides just the pay of army and as well as police officers in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But there was some assistance, economic assistance rendered to Serbia from Krajina and this is not something that should be overlooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly before the end of 1991, you know before the Vance Plan, you agree with me also that Serbia and Yugoslavia provided substantial support to the Serbs in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in October of 1991, in a statement I believe to the media, you had singled out Milosevic for his "immeasurable contribution towards finding a solution for the problems of the Krajina Serbs." Right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but it's possible. And I have to tell you that when I said those things, I did not speak for myself, but in my capacity as the minister of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can look at another document, please. This one, the doc ID of this is 02642959. It is quite a large document. I'm only interested really in one page, which is page 286 in the B/C/S and I think we just have an English translation of just that one page. Hopefully it's all in e-court. Yes, that's right. It should be page 286 there in the B/C/S. The ERN at the top will be 02643208. Yes. Exactly. If we could -- there, if we could centre on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, this is from the 6th of October, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, did you say there is an English version of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I hope there is, Your Honour. I believe it is coming. Sorry. I will wait.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English version is not accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's possible. Your Honour, and this is -- I suppose if it's anyone's fault it is mine. It was just a question of we get these things translated, sometimes they come in at the last minute and we send them to be uploaded, and there is simply not enough time to get everything done. It's really -- I am only interested in one line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And we will get a translation and put it into e-court as soon as we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, if will look at this, you will see that this is an article recording some statements by you on the 6th of October, 1991. And you see at the very end of the article, in bold, it says: "While supporting all decisions of the latest agreement in The Hague, Professor Macura stressed one more time 'the immeasurable contribution of Slobodan Milosevic towards finding the solution to the position of Serbs in the former Republic of Croatia'..." And that was your view at the time, in October of 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my hope, but it fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. Can you just read that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that statement expressed in hope or expressed in commending? Does it commend Milosevic or does it hope that Milosevic is going to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can read it one more time and then the witness can answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you can see, if you'll read along with me. It says: "While supporting all decisions of the latest agreement in The Hague, Professor Macura stressed one more time 'the immeasurable contribution of Slobodan Milosevic towards finding the solution to the position of Serbs in the former Republic of Croatia.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be expressing a hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, at that time you were speaking --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my perspective today, I say that this had been my hope, but it fell through. I'm not a lawyer, so you have an advantage over me there, but when I spoke about the nation and the ethnic minority, the nation is an entity that has the right to self-determination. This is what I spoke about when I spoke about the fact that Croats throughout Serbs from the constitution, because the Serbs as a constituent people would have the right to self-determination and to secede. This is what I was hoping, that Slobodan Milosevic would achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this has nothing to do with being a lawyer or not being a lawyer. Simple language. You are being quoted here. We are just looking at the language that you used. That language doesn't express hope. It doesn't matter how much you rant and rave in court here now. It doesn't express hope. You can see that, can't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What newspaper or publication is that, from which document comes from? Because it says Frankfurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As far as I can read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a newspaper published in Frankfurt, in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the name of the newspaper --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did not actually read this newspaper at all, ever. Novosti, that means news.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. In Novosti, or News, is the name of the newspaper. That's what it appears to be, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so I am clear, Mr. Macura, in October 1991 when you said these words you were talking about the immeasurable contribution of Slobodan Milosevic up and to and including that time. It wasn't something about the future. It was really about that time, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Rade Matijas is the journalist who signed this. Now I don't know whether he quoted me correctly. We would need to have the transcript to see whether I really said that, because this interview took half an hour, an hour, not five minutes. So I cannot claim with any certainty that these are my exact words. These are words that he may have put into my mouth. But at any rate, I thought that there would be a solution found and that I would not be among the remnants of a people that had been expelled and slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, just please try to focus on this, this issue of Mr. Milosevic's contribution.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In October 1991 you believed, didn't you, that Slobodan Milosevic had made an immeasurable contribution to the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I actually used the term "immeasurable," but it's possible. But at any rate, he did give his contribution. Without his help we would not have been able to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Exhibit number will be 949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have received the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. And, Your Honour, just so it is clear, and this is the same as last time, I am only interested in this page, not the entire range of B/C/S, and so we will, we will upload just that one page so there is no confusion in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just this page, the page and its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, even after the acceptance of the Vance Plan, it was still clear that Slobodan Milosevic and Serbia were the most important supporters of the Krajina Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the acceptance of the Vance Plan, I did not play any role, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to watch a short video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So if we could turn to the Sanction, please. Your Honours, this is -- the transcript of this clip is found at 65 ter number 2266, if that is helpful, but it is synchronised on the clip, as usual. At least I hope it is. If we could see that clip, now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, it was kind of a long clip. But you would -- well, first of all, this interview appears to be from around January of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that this was the time, because at that time we had a lot of activities in Krajina. And I was actually at the opposite end of the spectrum from Mr. Martic. I did not subscribe to what Mr. Martic said, because I had read the Vance Plan through; in fact, I translated it into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you had an opposite view. But it's accurate that Mr. Martic, at that time, was still fully supporting Mr. Milosevic and considered the contribution of Milosevic in Serbia to be the most important support of the Krajina Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from what has been said. This was said here quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we exhibit this video clip and the accompanying transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry? Are you tendering them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. And what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's just the clip and the transcript which is at 65 ter number 2266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And 65 ter number 2266, together with the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video clip will be Exhibit 950 and the transcript 951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, I believe you testified both that Milan Babic was opposed to the Vance Plan and that you, yourself, were also opposed to the Vance Plan. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In December of 1991, Milan Martic held that same view, and he also opposed the Vance Plan, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you know that at least initially, at one point, he opposed the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could -- I will show you Exhibit 518. I hope this is in the box. I hadn't necessarily anticipated showing this. I'm not sure if this was on the list of documents that we always send to Defence counsel. If it was not, I apologise. While we're waiting for this to come up on the screen, Mr. Macura, so that it's clear, Babic was opposed to the Vance Plan as it was conceived, although he would have supported it, if amended in certain ways?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Hopefully in a moment now we will have Exhibit 518 on the screen. Thank you. And if we could turn to the next page, please, in B/C/S. It is also the second page on the English. Mr. Macura, do you see that this is a document from the SAO Krajina, Ministry of the Interior, from the --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. It's from the 12th of December, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, if we can go to the last page, just to see the signature, briefly. Thanks. If you can scroll down to the bottom. That's the signature of Milan Martic as the author of this document, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So if we could go back to the second page, please. Thank you. If we could scroll down a little bit so that we can see the second and third paragraph. Perfect. We don't need to read it out, I guess, Mr. Macura, but if you can confirm to me. It says here that the Krajina Ministry of the Interior agrees with the position of the SAO Krajina government that peacekeeping forces could be deployed exclusively along the demarcation line. It says that in the second paragraph; correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph down it says that: "... any bringing of blue helmets," which is a reference to the UN peacekeepers, "... to the territory of SAO Krajina is out of the question. The SAO Krajina Ministry of the Interior rejects the proposal of Cyrus Vance." That's what it says, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So on the basis of this, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that in December of 1991 Milan Martic opposed the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. But I was not aware of the existence of this document. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand. Milan Martic subsequently changed gears and he supported -- he eventually supported the Vance Plan and the acceptance of the Vance Plan, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And he was persuaded to that view by Slobodan Milosevic, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And certainly by January of 1992, Martic openly supported the Vance Plan, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At that time we were practically on our way out from the political arena.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "we," who do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to Mr. Babic and his government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You would agree with me that Milan Martic had a different view than you did. He continued to view Slobodan Milosevic as the leader of all Serbs, all the way until he became RSK president in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, in fact, even during the presidential campaign in December of 1993 in January of 1994, he openly embraced Milosevic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him say things like that if he won the election, he would pass on the baton to the all Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic, or him to say that he was proud to call himself a Slobodan Milosevic man?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that statements to that effect had been made. But I can't now quote him verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. And Martic received support for his campaign from the Belgrade media, and from Serbia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Changing subjects a little bit, moving away from the Vance Plan. You testified that Milan Martic refused to consider the Z-4 plan unless or until the UNPROFOR mandate was extended, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He had good reason. He didn't want to discuss the Z-4 plan unless the mandate continued in the same -- with the same conditions, because Tudjman had announced that the current, the then mandate of the United Nations would have to cease existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And until that mandate was going to be extended, he didn't even want to consider the Z-4 proposal, not even really to look at it. Martic, I mean.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that was his position despite the fact that international representatives really urged him to consider the plan.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his opinion at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it correct or, if you know, that Martic rejected the Z-4 plan because Slobodan Milosevic told him to reject it.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At any rate, the UN mandate in Croatia was extended on the 31st of March, 1995, correct, and they changed the name and it became UNCRO instead of UNPROFOR. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But the essence was the same, both under the UNPROFOR and UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And even after that mandate was extended and the name was changed to UNCRO, Milan Martic still did not engage in negotiation of the Z-4 plan, did he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did, but I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, in fact, the insistence on the extension of the UNPROFOR mandate, it was kind of an excuse. He rejected the Z-4 plan because he wasn't willing to accept anything short of a separate state for the RSK. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your conclusion. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have a different view of it? Or you just don't know what his position was or his reasons at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I did not talk to him. I was not in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You yourself took a hard line position regarding the Z-4 plan. You considered it completely unacceptable, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. And I will tell you why, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you can be brief, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was a deception. This was not -- this was a trick. This was not an autonomy for Krajina, but just two districts, Glina and Knin. And this was not -- this did not cover even a fifth of Krajina, and the Knin and Glina districts were not even linked with the same -- they were not adjacent, and large portions of Slavonia and Lika remained outside of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. I'm going to ask you to look at another document, now. This document has the ERN ZA022624 to 2626. If we could see that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have a document ZA022614. Might that be the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It could be in that range and then I'm looking for the particular page. I apologise for the confusion. I see that that is the range that we have uploaded, so it is probably around page 10. If we could move forward until the page, until at the top of the page it has the ERN number ZA022624, please. All right. Thank you. And actually, it's the next page that I am mostly interested in. If we could pass to the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, if you look at this document with me, I'm sorry that it's only in English. But this is -- this is a memo which refers to a meeting between you and Grace Kang of the United Nations on the 2nd of March, 1995. Do you remember that meeting or having meetings with that person, around that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember this person, Grace Kang? Is that a name that you recall?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring any bells. I can't recall it at all. Then 15 years have passed, and I don't remember many things from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sure, I understand that it's been a while back. And if we could turn to the next page and focus on paragraph 5. Thank you. Mr. Macura, if you look there with me at paragraph 5 and tell me if this helps you remember the meeting. It says: "Macura expressed a hard-line attitude with respect to the Z-4 plan. It was unacceptable because it reduces RSK territory to 11 municipalities, leaving out towns such as Slunj. He also expressed dissatisfaction with the concept of autonomy within a Croatian state, particularly if autonomy does not include a separate military for the RSK. He said, 'What can you do with autonomy without an army?'" Do you remember expressing those positions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having expressed such positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It was, in fact, your position at the time that the Z-4 plan was unacceptable; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It definitely was my position that that plan was not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And was it -- and you were also dissatisfied with the idea of just accepting just autonomy within the Croatian state, if you couldn't have a separate RSK armed forces, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can only say that, that I expressed my personal views in that situation, but also, when I expressed my views as the minister of the information, I was practically subjected to the discipline of the SDS and the president, Milan Babic. I could give you interviews where I give my personal stories, which are different altogether. I was severely criticised when I told the journalist that I would accept to live within Croatia if it were a democratic -- country. And then I was harshly criticised at the Main Board meeting of the party who said that this was not the position of the party. Of course, you have the advantage here because you can, of course, extract what is -- what is that suits you, and of course I can tell you things that suit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, so that I'm clear, your rejection of the Z-4 plan, was that a personal position? Or was it your position as a holder of public office, or both?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not -- I was not holding at that time a public office, except that I was the president of the Committee for Foreign Relations in the Assembly. But it was certainly my position that the entire position -- the entire territory of the Krajina that was under our control should be part of that autonomy, rather than be compartmentalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay -- excuse me, sir. And was it your personal or sort of your public position that you were dissatisfied with the idea of autonomy if it didn't include an RSK military?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is still my position, because I couldn't trust the Croats, in view of our history and in view of everything that was transpiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about some other parts of this document while we have it up. First of all, before I do, who is Borislav Mikelic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borislav Mikelic was an old communist cadre. He discharged different political offices during the communist regime and he was also the director of a large meat-packing plant the Gavrilovic plant in Petrinja, and I know and knew him very well. He offered me two positions in his cabinet, that of the minister of information and that of the minister of education. But I wouldn't cooperate with him because I personally held a very -- had a very poor opinion of him, and secondly, I no longer wanted to be a part of the cabinet once the Vance Plan had been accepted, because I knew that there were no chances at all for Krajina's getting anything within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You know, you made reference to his cabinet. What was the public position or did Mr. Mikelic have a public position or public role in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain point in time Mr. Mikelic was the prime minister of the Krajina. I am not quite sure of the exact dates, from which date to which date, I can't say. But at any rate, he was a person who had dealings with the Croats on every possible front, be it trading in oil. He was a businessman. And that is in inverted commas, "a businessman."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's look at the prior page of the document, please, and I will focus your attention on paragraph 1. There it makes reference to the fact that this person Grace Kang said she had an informal meeting with you. And then it said you explained why Prime Minister Mikelic came under extreme political fire during the parliamentary session, including for a vote of no confidence. "'We think he is a good Croatian man," Macura said of Mikelic. Macura said he disliked the fact that Mikelic 'does business with the Croats.'
